The reed is made of cane, with a suitable springiness. The pads inside the tone holes are mostly soft leather or synthetic leather. The keywork is brass with silver or gold plating, for durability and agility. The whole design balances sound quality with durability.
上低音薩克斯常見於管樂團、室內樂、軍樂隊、大樂團、爵士小組合、搖滾樂團與行進樂隊: The baritone saxophone is common in wind bands, chamber music, military bands, big bands, small jazz groups, rock bands and marching bands. In classical line-ups it is a standard member of the wind band and the saxophone quartet, and it has appeared in works such as Richard Strauss's Symphonia Domestica, Bartók's The Wooden Prince, Gershwin's Rhapsody in Blue, Penderecki's The Devils of Loudun and Stravinsky's Ebony Concerto. In jazz it is a standard voice of the big band and appears in free jazz; the horn sections of pop, funk, blues, Latin and soul use it too, and Afrobeat bands often carry two players.

It is played with a single-reed mouthpiece, and the body is a conical tube of thin brass with a loop at the top to reduce its height; the modern instrument is usually in E-flat. Players are common in military bands, in the horn sections of musicals, rock and pop, and in big bands, jazz groups, concert wind bands, chamber music and marching bands.
上低音薩克斯由比利時製琴家 Adolphe Sax 於1846年創製，屬其十四件: The baritone saxophone was created by the Belgian instrument maker Adolphe Sax in 1846, one of his family of fourteen saxophones, intended to bridge woodwind and brass. The family divides into two groups of seven; an F baritone was designed but no example is known. The B♭ and E♭ group was the more successful because of its popularity in military bands. Early instruments keyed down to low B, a low B♭ mechanism was patented in 1887 and had become the majority standard by 1910. From the 1930s to the 1950s makers tried lengthening the bell to add a low A key, which was often badly in tune; from the late 1950s some low-A versions improved the tuning, and from the 1970s they gradually became standard. The highest keyed note was originally E♭, high F became standard in the 1920s, and high F♯ spread after the 1950s.
上低音薩克斯風音色渾厚深沉，帶有溫潤的金屬質感，既不如中音薩克斯明亮刺激，亦不若: The baritone saxophone has a full, deep timbre with a warm metallic quality, neither as bright and exciting as the alto nor as heavy and dull as the bass saxophone. Its range lies between the tenor and the bass saxophone; the low register is especially full and strong, the middle warm and soft, and the top rather dark. The instrument resonates in its own way and its sound carries, so it can make the bass part stand out clearly in a band. Against the trombone its timbre is rounder and softer; against the cello it has more of a modern metallic sheen. In a jazz band its full bass underlay is indispensable, and it usually gives the whole band's sound a firm foundation.
